facts_and_myths.claim: Niagara Falls produces enough renewable hydroelectric energy to power millions of homes across two countries.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Massive underground tunnels divert up to 75% of river flow to hydroelectric plants on both Canadian and American sides.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Annie Edson Taylor became the first person to survive going over the falls in a wooden pickle barrel in 1901 at age 63.

name: Victoria Falls
visual_anchor: Spectacular vertical 9:16 aerial perspective of the Zambezi River plunging into a deep basalt gorge, creating a massive rising cloud of shimmering mist.
core_traits: Colossal waterfall situated on the Zambezi River on the international border between Zambia and Zimbabwe
Known locally as 'Mosi-oa-Tunya' which translates to 'The Smoke That Thunders'
Forms the largest sheet of falling water on Earth based on its combined width (1,708 meters) and height (108 meters)
First documented by a Western explorer when Scottish missionary David Livingstone visited in 1855

facts_and_myths.claim: Victoria Falls is the highest single-drop waterfall in the world.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Angel Falls in Venezuela is the highest waterfall at 979 meters; Victoria Falls is celebrated instead for forming the widest unbroken curtain of falling water.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The mist spray from the cataract can shoot over 400 meters into the sky and is visible from up to 50 kilometers (30 miles) away.

facts_and_myths.claim: Swimmers can safely sit on the very precipice of the waterfall during low water seasons.
facts_and_myths.explanation: A natural rock depression called 'Devil's Pool' allows adventurous swimmers to lounge right at the cliff's edge without being carried over between August and January.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: On nights with a full moon, the spray from Victoria Falls creates an ethereal 'lunar rainbow' or moonbow.

name: Mount Everest
visual_anchor: Imposing vertical 9:16 telephoto shot of the windswept snow plume trailing off the razor-sharp pyramid summit of Mount Everest under an icy cobalt sky.
core_traits: Earth's highest mountain above sea level, reaching an official elevation of 8,848.86 meters (29,031.7 feet)
Located in the Mahalangur Himal sub-range of the Himalayas along the border of Nepal and Tibet, China
Known natively as Sagarmatha in Nepali ('Goddess of the Sky') and Chomolungma in Tibetan ('Mother Goddess of the World')
First officially summitted on May 29, 1953, by Sir Edmund Hillary of New Zealand and Tenzing Norgay Sherpa of Nepal

facts_and_myths.claim: Mount Everest is the furthest point on Earth's surface from the planet's center.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because the Earth bulges around the equator, Mount Chimborazo in Ecuador is actually 2,168 meters further from Earth's center than Everest.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Tectonic plate collisions continue to push Mount Everest upward by approximately 4 millimeters each year.

facts_and_myths.claim: Marine limestone and fossils from ancient seafloors are found near the summit of Mount Everest.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The upper pyramid is composed of Ordovician limestone formed beneath the ancient Tethys Ocean hundreds of millions of years before plate tectonics raised the Himalayas.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Above 8,000 meters lies the notorious 'Death Zone' where atmospheric oxygen levels are insufficient to sustain human life long term.

name: Burj Khalifa
visual_anchor: Gleaming vertical 9:16 view looking straight up the neo-futuristic stepped spire of the Burj Khalifa piercing the desert clouds above downtown Dubai.
core_traits: Neo-futuristic megatall skyscraper located in Downtown Dubai, United Arab Emirates
World's tallest building and freestanding artificial structure since its topping out in 2009, standing 828 meters (2,717 feet) tall
Designed by Adrian Smith at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) featuring a Y-shaped floor plan inspired by the Hymenocallis desert flower
Contains 163 floors including luxury residences, corporate suites, the Armani Hotel, and observation decks

facts_and_myths.claim: People on the top floors of the Burj Khalifa can watch the sunset twice in one evening.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Due to the tower's extreme height, you can watch the sun disappear at ground level, take the elevator to the top observation deck, and watch the sun set a second time.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The temperature at the top of the tower is approximately 6 degrees Celsius (11 degrees Fahrenheit) cooler than at ground level.

facts_and_myths.claim: The building sways by over 10 meters in severe desert windstorms.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The structural aerodynamics were tested extensively in wind tunnels; the tower deflects by only about 1.5 to 2 meters at its tip in heavy winds.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over 26,000 individually hand-cut glass panels make up the exterior curtain wall of the skyscraper.

name: Golden Gate Bridge
visual_anchor: Atmospheric vertical 9:16 perspective of the International Orange suspension towers of the Golden Gate Bridge rising above swirling low-lying Pacific fog.
core_traits: Iconic suspension bridge spanning the one-mile-wide Golden Gate strait connecting San Francisco to Marin County, California
Designed by engineers Joseph Strauss, Leon Moisseiff, and Charles Ellis, opening in 1937
Instantly recognized by its vibrant signature color known officially as 'International Orange'
Acclaimed as one of the Wonders of the Modern World by the American Society of Civil Engineers

facts_and_myths.claim: The Golden Gate Bridge is painted continuously from one end to the other all year round.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Bridge painters do not paint it continuously in a cycle; they perform localized touch-ups and targeted corrosion repairs where coastal salt air causes rust.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Its signature International Orange hue was originally just an anti-corrosive primer coat, but architect Irving Morrow loved it so much he made it permanent.

facts_and_myths.claim: The US Navy originally lobbied to paint the bridge in black and yellow stripes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Navy feared heavy San Francisco fog would obscure the bridge and proposed yellow and black stripes for marine navigation visibility.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over 80,000 miles of steel wire make up the two giant main suspension cables.

name: Empire State Building
visual_anchor: Classic vertical 9:16 shot of the Art Deco limestone spire of the Empire State Building piercing the misty Manhattan clouds, lit with vibrant night LED colors.
core_traits: 102-story Art Deco skyscraper situated in Midtown Manhattan, New York City, United States
Designed by Shreve, Lamb & Harmon and completed in 1931 during the Great Depression
Held the title of the world's tallest building for nearly 40 years until the World Trade Center opened in 1970
Immortalized in popular culture, most famously as the climbing tower for King Kong in 1933

facts_and_myths.claim: Dropping a penny from the observation deck of the Empire State Building can kill a pedestrian on the sidewalk.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because of air resistance and terminal velocity (around 30-50 mph), a falling penny flutters like a leaf and would at worst feel like a minor sting.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The skyscraper was constructed at breakneck speed, taking only 1 year and 45 days (410 days total) to complete.

facts_and_myths.claim: The mooring mast spire at the top was originally designed as a docking station for passenger airships (dirigibles).
facts_and_myths.explanation: Designers built the upper spire to moor transatlantic zeppelins, but treacherous thermal wind drafts over Manhattan made the idea too dangerous after one brief trial.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The building is struck by lightning an estimated 25 to 100 times every year.

name: Sagrada Familia
visual_anchor: Awe-inspiring vertical 9:16 interior shot of the Sagrada Familia with tree-like stone columns branching into the vaulted ceiling, flooded with kaleidoscopic stained-glass light.
core_traits: Monumental unfinished Roman Catholic minor basilica located in the Eixample district of Barcelona, Spain
Designed by renowned Catalan modernist architect Antoni Gaudi, who devoted his final decades to the project
Combines Catalan Modernism, Art Nouveau, and organic Gothic architectural styles
Under construction since 1882, making it one of the longest continuous architectural construction projects in modern history

facts_and_myths.claim: Antoni Gaudi is buried inside the crypt of the Sagrada Familia.
facts_and_myths.explanation: After being fatally struck by a tram in 1926, Gaudi was honored with a tomb placed directly within the chapel of El Carmen inside the basilica's crypt.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: When completed with its 172.5-meter central Jesus Christ tower, it will be the tallest religious church building in the world.

facts_and_myths.claim: The construction of the church has been heavily funded by the Spanish federal government.
facts_and_myths.explanation: As an expiatory temple, its construction has been financed entirely by private donations and ticket sales from millions of visiting tourists.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Gaudi deliberately set the height of the tallest spire at 172.5 meters so that man's creation would not surpass God's creation (Montjuic hill at 173 meters).

name: Louvre Museum
visual_anchor: Gleaming vertical 9:16 twilight view of I. M. Pei's illuminated glass and metal pyramid in the courtyard of the historic Renaissance Louvre Palace in Paris.
core_traits: World's most visited art museum and historic royal palace situated along the right bank of the Seine in Paris, France
Houses thousands of priceless masterpieces including Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa, Venus de Milo, and Winged Victory of Samothrace
Originally built as a medieval fortress under King Philip II in the 12th century before becoming a royal palace and museum in 1793
Features the famous modern glass entrance pyramid designed by Chinese-American architect I. M. Pei in 1989

facts_and_myths.claim: The glass pyramid of the Louvre was built with exactly 666 panes of glass to symbolize the devil.
facts_and_myths.explanation: This sensational conspiracy rumor was popularized by fictional thrillers; official museum documentation confirms there are exactly 673 glass panes (603 rhombi and 70 triangles).
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: If you spent 30 seconds viewing every single artwork in the Louvre, it would take you about 100 continuous days without sleeping.

facts_and_myths.claim: The Mona Lisa was once stolen from the Louvre by an Italian museum employee.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 1911, handyman Vincenzo Peruggia hid inside a broom closet and walked out with the Mona Lisa under his coat, believing the painting belonged back in Italy.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: During World War II, museum curators evacuated and hid over 3,000 priceless artworks in the French countryside to protect them from Nazi looting.

name: Saint Basil's Cathedral
visual_anchor: Vibrant vertical 9:16 view of the fairytale multicolored swirl onion domes of Saint Basil's Cathedral standing proudly on Red Square in Moscow under dusting snow.
core_traits: Distinctive Orthodox church situated at the southern end of Red Square in Moscow, Russia
Commissioned by Tsar Ivan the Terrible in the 1550s to commemorate the capture of Kazan and Astrakhan
World-famous for its nine brightly colored, geometrically patterned onion-shaped domes
Designed by architects Barma and Postnik Yakovlev as a visual earthly symbol of the Heavenly City of Jerusalem

facts_and_myths.claim: Ivan the Terrible ordered the architects blinded so they could never duplicate its astonishing beauty.
facts_and_myths.explanation: This is a popular folkloric legend without historical support; records show architect Postnik Yakovlev later designed walls for the Kazan Kremlin.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The cathedral is actually a cluster of nine independent small churches built around a central tenth core church.

facts_and_myths.claim: The cathedral was once slated for demolition by Joseph Stalin's urban planners.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Soviet planners wanted to raze the church to widen Red Square for military parades, but architect Pyotr Baranovsky heroically threatened suicide to save it.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The iconic multicolored candy-cane patterns were added over a century after original construction, which was originally plain white and gold.

name: Great Sphinx of Giza
visual_anchor: Majestic vertical 9:16 profile shot of the colossal limestone lion body and pharaoh head of the Great Sphinx guarding the sandy horizon before the Giza Pyramids.
core_traits: Monolithic limestone statue of a reclining mythical sphinx with the body of a lion and the head of a human pharaoh
Situated on the Giza Plateau on the west bank of the Nile River in Egypt, directly facing east
Carved from a single massive outcrop of natural limestone bed during the reign of Pharaoh Khafre around 2500 BC
Oldest known monumental sculpture in Egypt and one of the most recognizable statues in world history

facts_and_myths.claim: Napoleon Bonaparte's soldiers blew off the Sphinx's nose with a cannonball.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Drawings by Danish traveler Frederic Louis Norden made in 1737 prove the nose was already missing decades before Napoleon was even born.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: For centuries, shifting desert sands buried the Sphinx up to its shoulders until full modern excavation in the 1930s.

facts_and_myths.claim: Traces of original red and yellow paint still survive on the face and body of the Sphinx.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Chemical analysis of microscopic pigment residue confirms the Sphinx's face was originally painted vibrant red and the nemes headdress striped with blue and yellow.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The statue measures an impressive 73 meters (240 feet) long from paw to tail and 20 meters (66 feet) high.

name: Mount Rushmore
visual_anchor: Imposing vertical 9:16 low-angle view of the colossal 60-foot granite carved faces of four US presidents set against pine-forested Black Hills and a crisp blue sky.
core_traits: Colossal monumental sculpture carved into the granite face of Mount Rushmore in the Black Hills of South Dakota, United States
Depicts 60-foot-tall faces of four iconic US presidents: George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, Theodore Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln
Sculpted between 1927 and 1941 by Gutzon Borglum along with 400 skilled miners and stonecutters
Conceived to represent the birth, growth, preservation, and development of the United States

facts_and_myths.claim: Several workers died from falls and dynamite blasts during the 14 years of carving.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Despite precarious cliff scaffolding and explosive dynamite removal of 450,000 tons of rock, zero fatalities occurred during the entire project.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: About 90 percent of the rock removal was accomplished using precision dynamite charges detonated by skilled blasters.

facts_and_myths.claim: There is a hidden secret vault room carved into the mountain behind the presidential faces.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Gutzon Borglum created the 'Hall of Records', a secure granite canyon vault storing porcelain enamel panels inscribed with the US Constitution and Declaration of Independence.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Thomas Jefferson's face was originally started on Washington's right side, but flawed granite forced sculptors to dynamite it off and restart on the left.

name: Easter Island Moai
visual_anchor: Mysterious vertical 9:16 silhouette of giant stone Moai statues with long chiseled profiles standing in row along an ocean Ahu platform at sunset.
core_traits: Monolithic volcanic human figures carved by the indigenous Rapa Nui people on Easter Island in eastern Polynesia (Chile)
Carved between 1250 and 1500 AD to represent deified ancestral chiefs and protect their communities
Nearly 1,000 statues were produced, mostly quarried from compressed volcanic ash at Rano Raraku
Prominently featured oversized heads, prominent noses, deep eye sockets, and elongated earlobes

facts_and_myths.claim: The Moai are solely giant disembodied stone heads sitting on the ground.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Excavations have revealed that all Moai heads have complete torsos and bodies buried underground beneath centuries of sediment and topsoil.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Many Moai were fitted with inlaid white coral eyes and pupil discs made of black obsidian or red scoria.

facts_and_myths.claim: Oral traditions recount that the massive statues 'walked' to their coastal platforms.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Experimental archaeology demonstrated that teams of people rocking the statues from side to side with ropes can move upright Moai forward in a walking motion.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The largest completed Moai, nicknamed 'Paro', stands nearly 10 meters (33 feet) tall and weighs around 82 metric tons.

name: Alhambra
visual_anchor: Enchanting vertical 9:16 view through horseshoe arches into the Court of the Lions, with slender marble columns reflected in tranquil fountains.
core_traits: Stunning fortified palace and citadel complex perched on the Sabika hill overlooking Granada in Andalusia, Spain
Constructed primarily by the Nasrid Dynasty sultans in the 13th and 14th centuries as their royal court
Renowned as one of the finest surviving examples of Islamic Nasrid architecture and Moorish craftsmanship in Europe
Features the famous Court of the Lions, intricately carved stucco muqarnas, and lush Generalife gardens

facts_and_myths.claim: The Alhambra was completely leveled and rebuilt from scratch following the Christian Reconquista of 1492.
facts_and_myths.explanation: King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella preserved and maintained the palace because they were enchanted by its exquisite beauty, choosing it as their royal residence.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The name 'Alhambra' derives from the Arabic 'al-Hamra', meaning 'the red one', referring to the reddish clay of its outer fortress walls.

facts_and_myths.claim: The complex features poetic Arabic verses and geometric calligraphy carved across nearly every wall surface.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The walls feature thousands of inscriptions, including praise poems, Quranic verses, and the Nasrid motto: 'There is no conqueror but God'.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Its sophisticated mountain hydraulic systems have channeled fresh melting Sierra Nevada snow water through its courtyards for over 700 years.

name: Neuschwanstein Castle
visual_anchor: Fairytale vertical 9:16 aerial view of the white limestone spires and round turrets of Neuschwanstein Castle rising against the snowy Bavarian Alps and autumn forests.
core_traits: 19th-century historicist palace perched atop a rugged cliff above the village of Hohenschwangau in Bavaria, Germany
Commissioned by King Ludwig II of Bavaria as a theatrical romantic retreat dedicated to the operas of Richard Wagner
Iconic archetype of fairytale castle architecture that directly inspired Walt Disney's Cinderella and Sleeping Beauty Castle
Features Romanesque Revival styling with soaring turrets, gabled roofs, and a two-story Throne Hall

facts_and_myths.claim: Neuschwanstein Castle was constructed as a functional medieval military fortress.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It was built entirely as a romantic theatrical fantasy and private royal sanctuary in the late 1800s, lacking defensive military moats or fortifications.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Despite its medieval outward appearance, it featured revolutionary modern technology including central heating, telephone lines, and flush toilets.

facts_and_myths.claim: King Ludwig II was declared insane and deposed before the castle was even completed.
facts_and_myths.explanation: In 1886, Bavarian ministers declared Ludwig mentally unfit to rule due to his massive personal construction debts; he died mysteriously in Lake Starnberg days later.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The castle was opened to paying visitors just seven weeks after King Ludwig's death to pay off his accumulated debts.

name: Forbidden City
visual_anchor: Grand vertical 9:16 view across the marble terraces and crimson walls to the golden-tiled sweeping curved eaves of the Hall of Supreme Harmony in Beijing.
core_traits: Immense imperial palace complex located in the geographical center of Beijing, China
Served as the political ceremonial center and home of 24 Chinese emperors across the Ming and Qing dynasties from 1420 to 1912
Largest palace complex in the world, encompassing 980 surviving buildings and nearly 9,000 rooms over 72 hectares
Exemplifies traditional Chinese palace architecture with yellow glazed roof tiles, red walls, and strict south-north axial symmetry

facts_and_myths.claim: Common citizens were legally forbidden from entering the palace complex on pain of death.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because it was the sacred residence of the Son of Heaven, unauthorized ordinary subjects caught trespassing were subject to immediate execution.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Yellow was the exclusive imperial color of the Emperor, which is why nearly all roof tiles in the palace are glazed bright yellow.

facts_and_myths.claim: The palace buildings were built using massive quantities of iron nails to withstand earthquakes.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The timber structures were engineered entirely using intricate interlocking wooden mortise-and-tenon joints (dougong) without a single metal nail, allowing flexibility in quakes.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over one million laborers and 100,000 master artisans worked for 14 years to construct the imperial citadel.

name: Hollywood Sign
visual_anchor: Iconic vertical 9:16 view of the 45-foot-tall white sheet-metal letters spelling HOLLYWOOD across the chaparral scrub slope of Mount Lee overlooking Los Angeles.
core_traits: World-famous cultural icon and landmark spelling the word 'HOLLYWOOD' on Mount Lee in the Santa Monica Mountains, California
Originally erected in 1923 as a temporary illuminated outdoor billboard advertising an upscale real estate subdivision called 'HOLLYWOODLAND'
Features 45-foot-tall (13.7-meter) white steel capital letters spanning 350 feet across the hillside
Internationally recognized as the quintessential global symbol of the American cinema and entertainment industry

facts_and_myths.claim: The sign was originally intended to stand permanently as a monument to cinema.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It was built in 1923 as a temporary 18-month real estate advertisement for 'Hollywoodland'; the final 'LAND' was removed during a 1949 restoration.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Rock star Alice Cooper spearheaded a public 1978 campaign to rebuild the decaying sign, with Hugh Hefner and other celebrities funding individual letters.

facts_and_myths.claim: British actress Peg Entwistle tragically leaped to her death from atop the letter 'H' in 1932.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Devastated by career disappointments, the 24-year-old Broadway actress climbed a maintenance ladder to the top of the letter 'H' and jumped.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The sign is protected by 24/7 infrared security cameras, motion sensors, and razor-wire fencing to deter hikers and pranksters.

name: Times Square
visual_anchor: Dazzling vertical 9:16 night perspective of colossal animated LED billboards blazing light down upon bustling pedestrian plazas and yellow taxis at Times Square.
core_traits: Major commercial intersection, tourist destination, and entertainment hub in Midtown Manhattan, New York City
Located at the junction of Broadway and Seventh Avenue, stretching between West 42nd and West 47th Streets
Affectionately dubbed 'The Crossroads of the World', 'The Center of the Universe', and 'The Great White Way'
World-famous for its gigantic illuminated digital billboards, Broadway theaters, and annual New Year's Eve ball drop

facts_and_myths.claim: Times Square was originally named Longacre Square before being renamed in 1904.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It was renamed Times Square in April 1904 after The New York Times moved its headquarters to the newly constructed One Times Square skyscraper.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Billboards in Times Square consume an estimated 161 megawatts of electricity, enough to power 160,000 average homes.

facts_and_myths.claim: The giant New Year's Eve Waterford Crystal ball stays inside a hidden basement during the rest of the year.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The 12-foot, six-ton crystal ball remains perched atop the flagpole on the roof of One Times Square throughout the entire 365 days of the year.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Approximately 330,000 people pass through Times Square every single day, making it the most visited tourist attraction on Earth.

name: Tower of London
aliases: His Majesty's Royal Palace and Fortress of the Tower of London
visual_anchor: Imposing vertical 9:16 view of the medieval stone White Tower and fortified curtain walls on the north bank of the River Thames in central London.
core_traits: Historic fortified castle situated on the north bank of the River Thames in London, England
Founded in 1066 as part of the Norman Conquest by William the Conqueror, who built the central White Tower in 1078
Served historically as a royal residence, notorious prison, execution site, armory, and Royal Mint
Home to the British Crown Jewels, the Yeoman Warders (Beefeaters), and the ceremonial Ravens

facts_and_myths.claim: Hundreds of high-profile historical prisoners were publicly beheaded on the grassy green inside the Tower.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Only ten elite prisoners were executed on private Tower Green (including Anne Boleyn and Lady Jane Grey); most were executed outside on Tower Hill.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Legend holds that if the six resident ravens ever leave the Tower of London, the fortress and the kingdom will fall.

facts_and_myths.claim: The King's Guard and Yeoman Warders have guarded the fortress and Crown Jewels for centuries.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Yeoman Warders have safeguarded the Tower since 1485 and still perform the nightly 700-year-old 'Ceremony of the Keys' lockdown.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In medieval times, the Tower housed the Royal Menagerie, including lions, polar bears, and an elephant given as royal diplomatic gifts.

name: Tower Bridge
visual_anchor: Iconic vertical 9:16 low-angle shot of the neo-Gothic twin stone towers and blue suspension cables of Tower Bridge as its twin bascules lift for a ship on the Thames.
core_traits: Iconic combined bascule and suspension bridge crossing the River Thames close to the Tower of London in London, England
Engineered by Sir Horace Jones and Sir John Wolfe Barry, opening to traffic in 1894
Characterized by two towering neo-Gothic stone towers linked at the upper level by two horizontal high-level walkways
Features hydraulically powered bascules that open upward to let tall maritime ships navigate through

facts_and_myths.claim: American entrepreneur Robert McCulloch mistakenly bought London Bridge thinking he was buying Tower Bridge.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Both McCulloch and London officials repeatedly denied this urban legend, confirming he knew full well he was purchasing the 1831 granite London Bridge.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In 1952, a London double-decker bus driver had to accelerate and jump across a 3-foot opening gap when the bridge began lifting under his wheels.

facts_and_myths.claim: The bridge's original lifting mechanism was powered by pressurized steam hydraulics.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Massive steam engines pumped water into giant accumulators to raise the bascules within a minute, operating until converted to electro-hydraulics in 1976.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over 40,000 pedestrians and vehicles cross Tower Bridge every day.

name: Notre-Dame Cathedral
visual_anchor: Majestic vertical 9:16 view of the twin west facade towers and iconic round rose window of Notre-Dame Cathedral on the Ile de la Cite in Paris.
core_traits: Masterpiece of French Gothic architecture situated on the Ile de la Cite island in the River Seine in Paris, France
Began construction in 1163 under Bishop Maurice de Sully and largely completed by 1260
Famous for its revolutionary flying buttresses, ribbed vaulting, gargoyles, and stained-glass rose windows
Celebrated backdrop of Victor Hugo's famous 1831 novel 'The Hunchback of Notre-Dame'

facts_and_myths.claim: Victor Hugo wrote his famous novel specifically to help save the crumbling cathedral from demolition.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hugo wrote 'The Hunchback of Notre-Dame' to raise public awareness of Gothic heritage, sparking a massive national restoration campaign led by Viollet-le-Duc.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A bronze star in the plaza in front of the cathedral marks Point Zero, the origin marker from which all road distances in France are measured.

facts_and_myths.claim: The devastating fire of April 2019 completely destroyed all medieval stained-glass rose windows.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Miraculously, all three colossal 13th-century rose windows survived intact despite the collapse of the timber roof and spire.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Its giant 13-ton tenor bell named 'Emmanuel' has rung for major historical events since 1681, including the liberation of Paris in 1944.

name: Arc de Triomphe
visual_anchor: Heroic vertical 9:16 twilight view of the monumental neoclassical Arc de Triomphe at the center of Place Charles de Gaulle, glowing against streams of car headlights.
core_traits: Monumental neoclassical triumphal arch standing at the western end of the Champs-Elysees in Paris, France
Commissioned in 1806 by French Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte following his decisive victory at the Battle of Austerlitz
Honors those who fought and died for France in the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars
Houses France's Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and an eternal memorial flame beneath its central archway

facts_and_myths.claim: Napoleon Bonaparte marched his triumphant Grand Army through the completed arch after defeating Russia and Austria.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Construction was delayed and completed in 1836, fifteen years after Napoleon's death in exile; his body was carried beneath it during his 1840 state funeral.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In 1919, French aviator Charles Godefroy flew his Nieuport biplane straight through the arch to honor aviators killed in World War I.

facts_and_myths.claim: The eternal flame beneath the arch has burned continuously without being extinguished for over a century.
facts_and_myths.explanation: First lit on Armistice Day in 1923 at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, the flame is rekindled every evening at 6:30 PM and was never put out, even during Nazi occupation.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: All 12 grand avenues radiating from the traffic circle create a massive star pattern, which is why the square was originally named Place de l'Etoile (Star).

name: Sydney Harbour Bridge
visual_anchor: Grand vertical 9:16 view of the massive steel through-arch Sydney Harbour Bridge framing blue harbor waters, ferries, and the Sydney Opera House below.
core_traits: Steel through-arch bridge spanning Sydney Harbour, connecting the Sydney central business district with the North Shore
Engineered by British firm Dorman Long and designed under the supervision of John Bradfield, opening in 1932
Affectionately nicknamed 'The Coathanger' by locals because of its distinctive curved arch profile
One of the tallest and widest long-span steel arch bridges in the world, standing 134 meters above water level

facts_and_myths.claim: The four giant granite-clad concrete pylons at the ends support the primary weight of the bridge arch.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The pylons have zero structural purpose for supporting the steel arch; they were added purely for aesthetic balance and visual reassurance for the public.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: During hot Australian summer days, thermal expansion can raise the summit of the bridge arch by up to 18 centimeters (7 inches).

facts_and_myths.claim: Paul Hogan (the star of Crocodile Dundee) worked as a rigger and painter on the bridge before becoming an actor.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Hogan was employed for years as a bridge painter and rigger before launching his comedy television career.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It took 272,000 liters (72,000 gallons) of paint just to apply the bridge's initial three coats.

name: Hagia Sophia
visual_anchor: Breathtaking vertical 9:16 interior shot of Hagia Sophia looking up into the colossal floating dome surrounded by ring of light and historic golden mosaics.
core_traits: Monumental historic architectural marvel situated in the Sultanahmet district of Istanbul, Turkey
Built in 537 AD by Byzantine Emperor Justinian I as the imperial cathedral of Constantinople
Served as the world's largest cathedral for nearly 1,000 years before converting into an Ottoman mosque in 1453
Famed for its revolutionary massive central dome that seems to float unsupported on a ring of 40 arched windows

facts_and_myths.claim: Hagia Sophia was named in honor of a Christian female martyr named Saint Sophia.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The Greek name 'Hagia Sophia' translates to 'Holy Wisdom', referring directly to the divine personification of wisdom in Jesus Christ, not an individual saint.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Viking mercenaries serving in the Byzantine Emperor's Varangian Guard carved runic graffiti into the marble gallery parapets in the 9th century.

facts_and_myths.claim: The massive original dome collapsed during an earthquake just two decades after opening.
facts_and_myths.explanation: An earthquake in 558 AD compromised the shallow dome, prompting Isidore the Younger to rebuild it with a steeper pitch and stronger buttressing.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: It has functioned successively as an Eastern Orthodox cathedral, a Roman Catholic cathedral, an Ottoman imperial mosque, a secular museum, and back to a mosque.

name: Mount Kilimanjaro
visual_anchor: Spectacular vertical 9:16 wildlife scene with a herd of wild elephants grazing on golden savanna beneath the snow-capped flat dome of Mount Kilimanjaro.
core_traits: Dormant volcanic mountain located in northeastern Tanzania, near the border with Kenya
Highest mountain in Africa and the tallest single free-standing mountain above sea level in the world at 5,895 meters (19,341 feet)
Comprises three distinct volcanic cones: Kibo (the highest summit), Mawenzi, and Shira
Encompasses virtually every ecological climate zone on Earth, from tropical rainforest to arctic glaciers

facts_and_myths.claim: Mount Kilimanjaro's equatorial glaciers are expanding due to shifting Indian Ocean cloud patterns.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Scientific measurements show that Kilimanjaro's ancient summit glaciers have shrunk by more than 85 percent over the last century and may vanish in coming decades.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Because it is a non-technical walk-up climb, thousands of trekkers of varying experience attempt to reach Uhuru Peak each year.

facts_and_myths.claim: Almost every major ecological climatic zone can be experienced while hiking to the summit.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Climbers traverse five distinct ecological zones: cultivated farmland, rainforest, heather-moorland, alpine desert, and the arctic summit ice cap.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: In 1889, German geographer Hans Meyer and Austrian mountaineer Ludwig Purtscheller became the first recorded people to reach the summit.

name: Great Barrier Reef
visual_anchor: Stunning vertical 9:16 underwater shot of a vibrant green sea turtle gliding through crystalline turquoise waters above kaleidoscopic coral bommies.
core_traits: World's largest coral reef system, stretching over 2,300 kilometers (1,400 miles) along the coast of Queensland, Australia
Composed of over 2,900 individual reefs and 900 tropical islands in the Coral Sea
Largest single living structure on Earth, created by billions of tiny marine organisms called coral polyps
So colossal that it can be distinctly seen and photographed from outer space

facts_and_myths.claim: The Great Barrier Reef is composed of a single massive solid wall of coral rock.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It is a complex dynamic ecosystem of thousands of separate reefs, coral cays, mangrove estuaries, and deep marine channels.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Once a year in late spring, the entire reef participates in a synchronized mass coral spawning event triggered by water temperature and moonlight.

facts_and_myths.claim: The reef is home to over 1,500 species of marine fish and 400 species of hard coral.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It supports roughly 10 percent of the world's total fish species, alongside whales, dolphins, dugongs, and six species of threatened sea turtles.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The Great Barrier Reef is roughly the same physical land size as Italy or Japan.

name: Matterhorn
visual_anchor: Breathtaking vertical 9:16 alpine sunrise view of the razor-sharp pyramid peak of the Matterhorn glowing fiery golden above the pristine Riffelsee lake.
core_traits: Iconic pyramid-shaped mountain peak in the Pennine Alps, straddling the border between Switzerland and Italy
Stands 4,478 meters (14,692 feet) tall, overlooking the Swiss resort town of Zermatt
Famous for its steep, four-sided pyramidal horn facing the four cardinal compass directions
Universal symbol of the Swiss Alps and mountaineering, featured on Toblerone chocolate packaging for decades

facts_and_myths.claim: The Matterhorn is the highest mountain peak in the Alps.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Mont Blanc is the highest peak in the Alps at 4,808 meters; the Matterhorn is famous for its dramatic isolated pyramidal shape and steep climbing ridges.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Edward Whymper led the first successful ascent in 1865, which ended in tragedy when four climbers fell to their deaths on the descent.

facts_and_myths.claim: The distinctive bear hidden in the Toblerone mountain logo references the city of Bern.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Toblerone chocolate was created in Bern, known as 'The City of Bears', which is why a subtle bear silhouette is incorporated into the Matterhorn illustration.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The four distinct faces of the Matterhorn are so steep that snow cannot accumulate heavily, frequently causing massive avalanches down its flanks.

name: Iguazu Falls
visual_anchor: Spectacular vertical 9:16 panoramic shot looking directly into the deafening, horseshoe-shaped Devil's Throat gorge of Iguazu Falls surrounded by lush jungle.
core_traits: Monumental semicircular system of 275 individual waterfalls spanning the Iguazu River between Argentina and Brazil
Spans an astonishing 2.7 kilometers (1.7 miles) in width, surrounded by subtropical Atlantic rainforest
Centered on the awe-inspiring 'Devil's Throat' (Garganta del Diablo), a U-shaped chasm dropping 82 meters
Upon seeing Iguazu, US First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt famously remarked: 'Poor Niagara!'

facts_and_myths.claim: Iguazu Falls has a higher water volume and is wider than Niagara Falls.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Iguazu is nearly four times wider than Niagara and features 275 discrete drops, making it the most extensive waterfall system on Earth.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Depending on the rainy season, the number of individual cascades can range between 150 and nearly 300 waterfalls.

facts_and_myths.claim: The waterfalls are located entirely within Brazilian sovereign territory.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Approximately 80 percent of the waterfall falls within Argentina's national park, while Brazil offers the most expansive panoramic vistas across the river gorge.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The falls are home to thousands of great dusky swifts, small birds that fly straight through the crushing waterfalls to roost safely on the wet rock face behind.

name: Terracotta Army
visual_anchor: Atmospheric vertical 9:16 perspective looking down the excavated underground trench pits at hundreds of life-sized terracotta soldiers standing in formation.
core_traits: Vast subterranean army of thousands of life-sized terracotta warrior sculptures buried near Xi'an in Shaanxi province, China
Created in the late 3rd century BC to guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the first Emperor of a unified China, in the afterlife
Unearthed accidentally in 1974 by local farmers digging a water well
Comprises over 8,000 soldiers, 130 chariots with 520 horses, and 150 cavalry horses, each with unique facial features

facts_and_myths.claim: Every single terracotta warrior was mass-produced using identical uniform facial molds.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Master craftsmen individually sculpted each soldier's face, ears, hairstyle, and armor by hand, giving every warrior an entirely unique personality and expression.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The figures were originally painted with vibrant colored lacquers including pink, purple, blue, and red, which flaked away upon modern exposure to air.

facts_and_myths.claim: The actual burial mound of Emperor Qin Shi Huang has never been opened or excavated by archaeologists.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Fearing damage to unexcavated artifacts and respecting ancient accounts of toxic underground rivers of mercury, China has left the main tomb unsealed.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Soil samples taken around the imperial tumulus mound indeed revealed unusually high concentrations of toxic mercury.

name: Panama Canal
visual_anchor: Impressive vertical 9:16 view of a massive container ship squeezing through the Miraflores locks of the Panama Canal, flanked by lush tropical rainforest.
core_traits: 82-kilometer (51-mile) artificial waterway in Panama connecting the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean across the Isthmus of Panama
Constructed initially by France and finished by the United States, officially opening for maritime trade in 1914
Uses a stepped gravity-fed lock system that lifts cargo ships 26 meters (85 feet) up to artificial Gatun Lake and down again
One of the greatest and most difficult engineering feats of the 20th century, shaving 8,000 nautical miles off voyages around Cape Horn

facts_and_myths.claim: The Atlantic Ocean end of the canal is west of the Pacific Ocean end due to the S-shaped curvature of Panama.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Because of the winding geography of the Isthmus of Panama, ships traveling from the Atlantic to the Pacific travel from northwest to southeast.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Over 25,000 workers died from yellow fever, malaria, and landslides during the French and early American construction eras.

facts_and_myths.claim: Saltwater from the Atlantic and Pacific oceans mixes directly together inside the canal locks.
facts_and_myths.explanation: The canal relies entirely on fresh rainwater stored in artificial Gatun Lake to operate the gravity-fed locks, meaning fresh water flushes outward to both oceans.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The lowest toll ever paid was 36 cents by American adventurer Richard Halliburton, who swam the entire length of the canal in 1928.

name: Mont-Saint-Michel
visual_anchor: Magical vertical 9:16 view of the fairytale tidal island abbey of Mont-Saint-Michel rising above shimmering sandbanks and incoming Atlantic tides at sunset.
core_traits: Medieval abbey and fortified island commune situated in a vast tidal bay in Normandy, France
Perched dramatically atop a rocky granite outcrop topped by a Romanesque and Gothic abbey dedicated to Archangel Michael
Famous for experiencing some of the most extreme and rapid tidal variations in continental Europe
Surrounded entirely by treacherous tidal waters at high tide and exposed quicksand mudflats at low tide

facts_and_myths.claim: The ocean tide in Mont-Saint-Michel bay rushes in as fast as a galloping horse.
facts_and_myths.explanation: While popularized by author Victor Hugo, the tide actually advances at about 3 to 4 miles per hour (walking speed), though its rapid rise across flat sand quickly traps unwary walkers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: During the French Revolution, the historic abbey was turned into a high-security prison nicknamed the 'Bastille of the Sea'.

facts_and_myths.claim: The fortress island successfully resisted English sieges for over 30 years during the Hundred Years' War.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Protected by its massive defensive walls, treacherous tides, and quicksand, a small garrison of French knights repelled repeated English military assaults.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: A golden statue of Saint Michael slaying a dragon crowns the soaring 91-meter-high abbey spire.

name: Table Mountain
visual_anchor: Majestic vertical 9:16 wide-angle view of the dramatic flat-topped sandstone cliff of Table Mountain draped in its white cloud 'tablecloth' above Cape Town.
core_traits: Prominent flat-topped mountain forming a dramatic landmark overlooking the city of Cape Town in South Africa
Features an expansive level plateau approximately 3 kilometers (2 miles) from side to side, rising 1,086 meters above sea level
One of the oldest mountains on Earth, with sandstone base rocks estimated at over 300 million years old
Known for the spectacular orographic white cloud cascade that blankets its summit, famously called the 'tablecloth'

facts_and_myths.claim: Table Mountain is among the most biologically diverse floral hotspots on the planet.
facts_and_myths.explanation: It is home to over 2,200 plant species in the Cape Floral Region, containing more plant diversity than the entire United Kingdom.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: Local folklore attributes the cascading cloud 'tablecloth' to a pipe-smoking contest between a pirate named Van Hunks and the devil.

facts_and_myths.claim: The flat top of Table Mountain was created by ancient volcanic lava plateau eruptions.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Table Mountain is not volcanic; its flat plateau was sculpted over hundreds of millions of years by wind and water erosion of hard horizontal sandstone layers.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: The modern cable car to the summit features a rotating floor that offers passengers a 360-degree panoramic view during the ascent.

name: Brandenburg Gate
visual_anchor: Solemn vertical 9:16 view of the neoclassical sandstone columns of the Brandenburg Gate crowned by the bronze Quadriga chariot at dusk in Berlin.
core_traits: 18th-century neoclassical sandstone triumphal monument located in Mitte, Berlin, Germany
Commissioned by Prussian King Frederick William II and designed by Carl Gotthard Langhans, completed in 1791
Crowned by the iconic bronze sculpture of the Quadriga, a chariot drawn by four horses driven by the goddess of peace (later victory)
Historic symbol of German division during the Cold War (standing inside the Berlin Wall buffer) and the ultimate emblem of German reunification

facts_and_myths.claim: Napoleon Bonaparte stole the bronze Quadriga chariot from the top of the gate and hauled it back to Paris.
facts_and_myths.explanation: After conquering Prussia in 1806, Napoleon took the Quadriga to Paris as a war trophy, where it remained until Prussian troops reclaimed it in 1814 after Waterloo.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: US President Ronald Reagan delivered his famous 1987 speech in front of the gate, declaring: 'Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!'

facts_and_myths.claim: The Brandenburg Gate was completely demolished by Allied bombing in World War II and rebuilt from scratch.
facts_and_myths.explanation: Although heavily damaged and pockmarked by artillery and bullets, the gate's columns survived the war and were carefully restored by East and West Berlin authorities.
facts_and_myths.fun_fact: During the Cold War, the gate stood in no-man's land directly behind the Berlin Wall, inaccessible to citizens of both sides.
